newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota seeks global prestige with New York listing.
newsitem.headline: Toyota seeks global prestige with New York listing.

text.p: Japanese car giant Toyota Motor Corp expressed a strong desire on Tuesday to polish up its international profile with a renewed push to list on the New York Stock Exchange.

The company said it hopes to enhance its reputation as a global enterprise by joining 11 other big-name Japanese companies listed on the exchange, including its rival Honda Motor Co Ltd, the sole car maker among them.

"We're positively looking into the possibility, but we have not yet decided anything concrete. We have not set any target year for the move," a Toyota spokesman said, when asked about a media report that Toyota is seeking the listing by 2000.
Toyota plans to set up an internal team to deal with the necessary listing procedures, the spokesman said.

Despite being Japan's biggest car company and the country's most profitable firm, Nagoya-based Toyota still has something of a "country cousin" reputation and is regarded by some in the industry as a conservative business.
Toyota, which is stepping up its business in North America, would be able to diversify its sources of funds for new projects by listing its shares in New York.

But Toyota, which has hefty funds in the form of cash and deposits worth 2.4 trillion yen ($20.3 billion), said it is seeking global status rather than concrete benefits. "The purpose is to gain a reputation as a 'global corporation' rather than seeking to raise funds," said the spokesman.

On Tuesday, Toyota's president Hiroshi Okuda was quoted as telling the mass-circulation daily Yomiuri Shimbun in an interview that the company hopes to list its shares in New York by 2000 to improve its global image.

"The issue of disclosure would be difficult," Okuda was quoted as saying. But he added: "We have already reached an internal consensus that doing so is necessary for the purpose of our public relations. We hope to be listed by 2000."
Toyota would come under strict scrutiny from the Securities Exchange Commission (SEC) and would need to win the body's approval for the listing.
Toyota has set 2000 as the target because it believes it will be able to present itself to investors as a global company by then, the newspaper report said.
The carmaker is due to complete its current business plan for expanding overseas production this year and is looking to expand output in China and India by 2000, it said.

Toyota and other Japanese car makers have shifted manufacturing offshore to sites with low operating costs and proximity to markets. In the first six months to September, about 30 percent of Toyota's car output was overseas.

Even in non-car areas, Toyota may go global by forging an alliance with American and European telecommunications firms in an attempt to diversify into new, lucrative niches, away from its mainstay operations, industry sources say.

"Listing in New York is a symbolic action at a time when Toyota is set to accelerate its U.S. output in coming years and seek real globalisation of its operations," said Kazunori Tokuda, an analyst at Wako Research Institute of Economics.
"I cannot predict what will happen after the listing, but speaking optimistically, the listing would be good as Toyota's higher overseas output may lead to more group sales," he said.
But the U.S. market may move into a cyclical slump in 1998, and Toyota may suffer weak earnings, which in turn may delay the timing of its listing, he said.
"The outlook is not all good," he said.

On Tuesday, Toyota's shares rose 40 yen to 3,200 yen ($27) while the key Nikkei market average suffered a moderate fall. Blue-chips such as Toyota have stayed strong despite the overall gloom gripping the Tokyo stock market. ($1=118 yen)
